# Judith Chapter 12 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Judith 12 (20 verses)
**Theme:** Judith in the Assyrian camp; Holofernes' banquet; the eve of the climax

---

## Disagreement Count: 16

---

### Disagreement 1 — Verse 2: "offense" vs. "violation"

**EMET:** "lest there be an offense"
**LOGOS:** "lest it be an offense to me"
**PNEUMA:** "It would be a violation"

**Issue:** Greek skandalon — a stumbling block, trap, or cause of offense. Here specifically a religious violation. PNEUMA's "violation" is strong and clear; EMET/LOGOS have "offense." The personal dimension ("to me" in LOGOS) is actually present in some manuscripts.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Lest it be an offense to me" — personal dimension included, skandalon preserved as "offense."

---

### Disagreement 2 — Verse 3: Holofernes' concern about resupply

**EMET:** "where will we get more to give you the same?"
**LOGOS:** "where can we procure more of the same kind to provide for you?"
**PNEUMA:** Collapses to a frown and a question, omitting "of the same kind"

**Issue:** Holofernes' concern is specifically about kosher food — he understands (partially) what her requirements are. The "same kind" matters.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Where can we get more of the same kind to provide for you?" The theological detail retained.

---

### Disagreement 3 — Verse 4: "purposed" vs. "determined" vs. "planned"

**EMET:** "what he has purposed"
**LOGOS:** "what he has determined"
**PNEUMA:** "what he has planned"

**Issue:** Greek ebouleuato (from bouleuō, counsel/plan/determine). "Purposed" preserves the sense of deliberate will. All are adequate.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "What he has purposed" — slightly more elevated, appropriate to the solemnity of the oath.

---

### Disagreement 4 — Verse 5: Judith's sleeping hours

**EMET:** "she slept until the middle of the night"
**LOGOS:** "she slept until midnight"
**PNEUMA:** "she slept until the middle of the night"

**Issue:** Minor phrasing variation. LOGOS' "midnight" is slightly more natural in English; EMET/PNEUMA more literal to heos mesēs nyktos.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "She slept until midnight" — natural English idiom without loss.

---

### Disagreement 5 — Verse 7: "bodyguards" vs. "guard"

**EMET:** "his bodyguards"
**LOGOS:** "his guard"
**PNEUMA:** "his guards"

**Issue:** Greek phylakas — watchers, guards. "Bodyguard" implies personal protection detail specifically; "guard" is more general.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "His guard" — general enough to cover the perimeter guards who regulated camp access.

---

### Disagreement 6 — Verse 8: "direct her way" vs. "show her the path"

**EMET:** "to direct her way for the uplifting of the sons of his people"
**LOGOS:** "to direct her way for the raising up of the sons of his people"
**PNEUMA:** "to show her the path — to lift up the sons of his people"

**Issue:** Greek kateuthunai tēn hodon autēs. "Direct her way" vs. "show her the path." The prayer is for divine guidance. PNEUMA breaks it into two clauses; EMET/LOGOS keep it as a single infinitive phrase.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "To direct her way for the uplifting of the sons of his people" — literal structure retained; "uplifting" preferred over "raising up" for register.

---

### Disagreement 7 — Verse 10: "personal servants" vs. "servants alone"

**EMET:** "a banquet for his servants alone"
**LOGOS:** "a banquet for his personal servants alone"
**PNEUMA:** "a private banquet for his personal attendants"

**Issue:** The Greek tois idiois paisi — "his own servants/boys." "Personal servants" is more specific; "alone" distinguishes them from officers.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "A banquet for his personal servants alone" — both qualifiers retained.

---

### Disagreement 8 — Verse 11: Bagoas' role description

**EMET:** "who had charge of all his affairs"
**LOGOS:** "who had charge of all his affairs"
**PNEUMA:** "who managed all his personal affairs"

**Issue:** All agents agree on the substance. PNEUMA adds "personal" — a reasonable inference but not in the text.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Who had charge of all his affairs" — without the addition.

---

### Disagreement 9 — Verse 12: Explicit language about Holofernes' intentions

**EMET:** "without having intercourse with her"
**LOGOS:** "without lying with her"
**PNEUMA:** "without sleeping with her"

**Issue:** Greek syngenesthai ("to come together with"). EMET renders most literally with "intercourse"; LOGOS uses the older English euphemism "lying with"; PNEUMA uses the modern euphemism "sleeping with."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Without lying with her" — the traditional biblical idiom is appropriate to the register of the translation and is unambiguous without clinical bluntness.

---

### Disagreement 10 — Verse 12: "seduce" vs. "win her over"

**EMET:** "seduce her"
**LOGOS:** "win her over"
**PNEUMA:** "win her over"

**Issue:** Greek katagoēseumen — to enchant, beguile, win by deception. "Seduce" carries specifically sexual connotations; "win over" is more neutral. The context is sexual, making "seduce" accurate.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Win her over" — the less charged reading; the context makes the meaning clear without the word "seduce" doing double duty for the sexual and persuasive meanings.

---

### Disagreement 11 — Verse 13: Bagoas' opening line

**EMET:** "Let the fair young woman not be reluctant to come"
**LOGOS:** "Let this fair young woman not hesitate to come"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't let this beautiful young woman be too shy to come"

**Issue:** Greek mē oknēsatō — "let her not hesitate/shrink from." PNEUMA's "too shy" is somewhat colloquial. LOGOS' "hesitate" is cleanest.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Let this fair young woman not hesitate to come."

---

### Disagreement 12 — Verse 14: "with haste" vs. "at once"

**EMET:** "I will do with haste"
**LOGOS:** "I will do at once"
**PNEUMA:** "I will do at once"

**Issue:** Greek meta spoudēs — "with speed/haste." "With haste" is literal; "at once" is natural English.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "I will do at once" — English idiom preferred.

---

### Disagreement 13 — Verse 15: Judith's preparation scene

**EMET:** "adorned herself with her clothing and all her feminine adornment"
**LOGOS:** "dressed herself in her garments and all her woman's adornment"
**PNEUMA:** "put on her full array — her clothes, her jewelry, every piece of her feminine adornment"

**Issue:** PNEUMA specifies "jewelry" not in the Greek at this point (the Greek says kosmō gynaikeiō, "woman's adornment/cosmetics"). The author is deliberate about not itemizing — the point is totality.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Dressed herself in her garments and all her woman's adornment" — complete but not inventoried.

---

### Disagreement 14 — Verse 16: Holofernes' internal state

**EMET:** "his heart was ravished... his soul was stirred"
**LOGOS:** "his heart was ravished... his soul was shaken with desire"
**PNEUMA:** "his heart was seized — completely undone"

**Issue:** Two distinct Greek phrases: psychē autou etarachthē ("his soul was agitated/shaken") and the heart metaphor. PNEUMA collapses them into one. The distinction between heart and soul is meaningful.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "His heart was ravished at the sight of her. His soul was shaken with desire" — both clauses retained distinctly.

---

### Disagreement 15 — Verse 18: "magnified" vs. "exalted" vs. "lifted higher"

**EMET:** "my life is magnified this day"
**LOGOS:** "today my life is exalted"
**PNEUMA:** "Today my life has been lifted higher"

**Issue:** Greek emegalunthē — from megalynō, to make great/magnify/exalt. This is the same word used in the Magnificat (Luke 1:46, "my soul magnifies the Lord"). LOGOS' "exalted" is elegant; EMET's "magnified" preserves the root connection.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "My life is exalted above all my days" — "exalted" preferred for register and irony (the Magnificat echo works both ways here).

---

### Disagreement 16 — Verse 20: Description of Holofernes' drinking

**EMET:** "drank very much wine — more than he had ever drunk in one single day"
**LOGOS:** "drank a great quantity of wine — more than he had drunk on any single day"
**PNEUMA:** "drank more wine that night than he had drunk on any single day of his entire life"

**Issue:** The Greek is emphatic: pampoly — "very much" or "a great amount." PNEUMA adds "of his entire life" — that is implied by "since he was born" in EMET/LOGOS.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Drank a great deal of wine — more than he had drunk on any single day since he was born." The chronological phrase "since he was born" is meaningful parallel to v. 18's same phrase about Judith.

---

## Summary

Total disagreements: 16
Key scenes: Three-day prayer routine (vv. 7-9), the banquet invitation (vv. 10-14), the climactic evening (vv. 15-20)
Theologically significant: v. 18 Magnificat echo (emegalunthē); v. 4 oath by Holofernes' "soul"; v. 12 explicit statement of threat
Structural note: The chapter ends at maximum narrative tension — the trap is set, the predator is drunk, the instrument of God is in position.
